32.0.s.en: (1) The two tribes' request for the land and Moses' answer to them

32.0.0.en: The land of Jazer: one of the cities of the land of Gilead.

32.0.1.en: The land of Gilead: a region that included all the east of the river Jordan, famous for its trees and pastures that run through its mountains, for it is a mountainous region, and among its mountains some green plains were spread (Map 3). The leaders and heads of the tribes of Reuben and Gad looked toward the land east of the Jordan, part of which the Midianites had inhabited, and seeing that it was a land rich in valleys and fertile pastures, suitable for grazing cattle, they came to Moses the leader of the people and Eleazar the high priest with their request, mentioned in the following verses.

32.1.0.en: This verse includes the names of some cities and villages of the region of Gilead, the subject of the leaders' speech with Moses and Eleazar. The most important is the city of Heshbon, the capital of the land of the Amorites, and it and the rest of the lands mentioned lie east of the Dead Sea and southeast of the river Jordan.

32.1.1.en: Ataroth: it no longer exists today, and it is thought that it was between Heshbon, the capital of the Amorites, and the city of Dibon.

32.1.2.en: Dibon: it was one of the cities of the Moabites, and the Amorites took it, and then the children of Israel took it from them. Jazer: a city with some small villages belonging to it, lying west of Ammon, a city of the Amorites. Heshbon: the capital of Sihon king of the Amorites.

32.1.3.en: Shebam: a city considered adjoining and an extension of Heshbon on the north.

32.1.4.en: Elealeh: a city lying north of Heshbon also.

32.1.5.en: Nebo: a mountain city that took its name from Mount Nebo.

32.1.6.en: Beon: also called Meon, and also "Baal-meon".

32.2.0.en: As for the subject of the request and the speech, it is a petition from the tribes of Reuben and Gad to take this land as their portion and be content with it, and not cross the Jordan with the rest of the tribes. Their request to Moses was accompanied by an explanation that the number of the cattle of these two tribes was very great, and that these lands were the most suitable lands for them and their cattle. The expression "the country which the Lord smote before the congregation of Israel" is a gracious expression in which they ascribed the war and the victory to God and not to their own arm.

32.2.1.en: It is also noted that their request was presented in a humble and gentle form, for they said, "if we have found grace in thy sight", which is a courteous expression of asking leave in which they set aside their own will and declare their desire but leave the matter to Moses. Would that we too learned such a manner in the matters of our lives when we ask for something.

32.3.0.en: Moses held back from the request of the tribes of Reuben and Gad and told them what was within him with some disapproval!! .. Is it fitting that you take the land and settle with your cattle while the rest of the tribes go out to the wars of liberating the land and possessing it? Moses used the expression "your brethren" because of the shared responsibility it carries for all, since the work is one work, and also because this expression may embarrass the two tribes in their request. Moses put Gad before Reuben either because they were the owners of the idea, or because of their taking the lead in speaking about the sons of Reuben, besides the fact that Reuben lost the birthright and precedence over his brothers because of his sin with his father's wife.

32.4.0.en: Moses continues his speech and points out a new fault in this request, which is that if he allowed them to do so, they would be the cause of the remaining tribes' becoming slack. Why should the others fight while you are here at ease?!

32.5.0.en: In these verses Moses began a severe and decisive speech with the delegates and heads of the two tribes, and this speech can be summarized in the following points:

32.5.1.en: 1- He reminds them that what they want to do here, "to possess the land", and its result in weakening the people's resolve, is the same as their fathers did when they spied out the land, as if history were repeating itself.

32.5.2.en: 2- He recalls to them what bears on the matter of spying out the land, and how, when the spies returned, they discouraged and disheartened the people from going forward to take the land.

32.5.3.en: 3- He also reminds them that this earlier cowardly stand led to God's anger against His people and His oath that none of them should enter the land (chs. 13-14).

32.5.4.en: 4- The result of this anger was the people's wandering for forty years in the wilderness and the perishing of the whole wicked generation that doubted God's power and feared the peoples of the land.

32.5.5.en: 5- Moses did not fail to add a parenthetical remark that this punishment did not include Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, the two faithful men who took a position different from the rest of the spies (v. 12).

32.6.0.en: Moses increases the sharpness of his manner and tone in speaking with the leaders. He begins by rebuking them for this very selfish idea, and adds that he sees them as he saw their fathers of old, and describes them as sinners, "an increase of sinful men", and that by such a request they will bring the anger of God upon the people once again, as happened of old, so that this whole people will perish because of them.

32.6.1.en: Leadership, whatever its level, even at the level of the family, requires the leader at times to take decisive positions in order to protect others. Decisiveness is not a fault in itself as long as love and counsel accompany it. Rather, slackness and lack of decisiveness is considered sin if a person neglects a wrong and is lax about it, especially if he is in charge.

32.7.s.en: (2) The second speech of the two tribes and Moses' conditional agreement

32.7.1.en: After listening to Moses' rebuke, the heads of the two tribes did not leave, but continued speaking with Moses, presenting their point of view, which was as follows: allow us to build here folds for our cattle, and to build houses in fenced cities so that they may be strong, and to put in them our little ones and our wives. When this is done we shall be the first men to go forward, ready and ahead of the others, to war for our people Israel, so that they too may possess their portions of the land west of the river Jordan.

32.8.0.en: "And we will not return to our homes which you have given us until we are fully assured that every tribe has received by lot what God has apportioned to it, and we shall not possess anything with them in the new land west of the river Jordan, but shall be content with what we have taken of the land east of it."

32.9.0.en: As for Moses, after hearing their new idea, his answer was this: if you hold to all these words and fulfill your covenant, to prepare for fighting and war and even to go ahead of the rest of the tribes in advancing to war, and when God calls you to take part with your brethren in liberating the land you cross the Jordan with all your men armed for war, until the complete victory is achieved and God subdues all the peoples dwelling west of the Jordan to His people, then this land will be your possession as you wished, and keeping your promise will clear you of God's anger and vengeance. Note: the expression "before the Lord" (v. 20) means that these two tribes should take their position in the wars in the front ranks before the ark of the covenant, which represents the divine presence, and which the people took with them in most of their wars.

32.10.0.en: The rest of Moses' speech was also a warning to them of what would befall them if they did not fulfill their covenant, and were slack and did not take part with the people in the fighting, for this would be a shameful act on their part and would expose them to God's anger and vengeance, because this covenant and this promise were before God and He is the witness to it. We note here that Moses, before giving them permission and his agreement (v. 24), repeats his previous warning (vv. 10-11) so as to make their promise firm upon them and make them afraid of going back, and at the same time to clear himself of responsibility for the consequence of their going back on fulfilling their covenant, which would expose them to the wrath of God.

32.11.0.en: These were the words of Moses' agreement and his permission to them to build folds for the cattle and to build cities for the dwelling of their wives and children.

32.12.0.en: As a kind of thanks, and very humbly, the heads of the tribes of Gad and Reuben gave thanks to Moses and pledged to do all that they had promised and all that Moses had permitted them.

32.13.0.en: Likewise, for the last time, they renewed their covenants to number all the men prepared for war and keep them in a state of constant readiness, and to leave their wives and cattle in the cities of Gilead, that is, the lands of the Moabites and Midianites.

32.14.0.en: After the agreement had become final, Moses directed his words to the leaders of the people and the representatives: Eleazar the high priest, Joshua the son of Nun the supreme commander, and the heads of the tribes, who were the representatives of all the people. Moses' words to all carried a review of all the preceding speech, and made clear to them that his consent was a conditional consent, that all were witnesses to what the heads of the two tribes had pronounced, and that all also had authority over this agreement as to its validity or its annulment, and all this depended on how far the two tribes kept to what they had said and promised. If they took part in the fighting and crossed the Jordan with their men of war, and all the tribes took possession of their portions, this land would be theirs, that is, the tribes of Gad and Reuben's. But if they broke their promise, this land would not be given to them but taken from them, and they would share by lot with the rest of the tribes the land that is west of the Jordan.

32.15.0.en: These two verses carry the same as what the heads of the two tribes had pledged before, and its repetition here is to confirm their commitment to it. Joshua reminded them of their promise after the death of Moses, and they crossed and fought with their brethren, and after the end of the war he thanked them for keeping their promise, and then they returned to their lands east of the Jordan (Josh 1:12-18, 22:1-9).

32.16.0.en: The cities of the country round about: that is, the cities and the borders extending around them.

32.16.1.en: Although the tribe of Manasseh did not take part in all the preceding dialogue and asked nothing of Moses, we find that when Moses granted the land to the tribes of Gad and Reuben, he associated with them in this land half the tribe of Manasseh, perhaps because he found this land too large to belong to the two tribes alone. We also understand from the context the agreement of the heads of the clans of the tribe of Manasseh to this, since half of the tribe did in fact possess land east of the Jordan.

32.16.2.en: As for the land that was the subject of all the discussion, it was, as already explained, the land of the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, the land extending along the east of the river Jordan from its north to its south.

32.16.3.en: We must not fail to mention here that although Moses agreed with the two tribes on their choice, this does not free the two tribes from the suspicion of selfishness, for they set themselves apart and chose the land by their own will and did not wait for the Lord's choice or His lot. In any case, these two tribes paid the price of their haste and greed .. for they were relatively cut off from the rest of the people because of the river Jordan (the natural divide) and became exposed to harassment by many of the peoples of the region throughout their history ..

32.16.4.en: Would that you not be hasty, nor greedy, nor go ahead of your brethren in choosing, but wait for the portion the Lord has for you.

32.17.s.en: (3) The rebuilding of the land after obtaining it

32.17.0.en: The books also carry a historical and geographical record of the people of God, and for this reason we find that the coming verses are all a record of the names of the cities that the two tribes and half the tribe of Manasseh rebuilt and built. However, honesty requires us to say that after research we found that most of these "villages", which are called here "cities", either disappeared, were changed or were annexed.

32.17.1.en: Also, given the lack of precise maps showing the reader the location of these very small cities, and the resort of the most careful commentators to the expressions "perhaps it is" or "perhaps it has now become", we content ourselves here with a general reference to these cities, mentioning in detail only what is certain.

32.17.2.en: Verses (34-36) include the cities that the tribe of Gad rebuilt and took, which were originally cities (villages) of the Amorites, and they were:

32.17.3.en: 1- Dibon: it was taken from the Amorites and was afterward called "Dibon-gad" after the tribe of Gad. But Joshua afterward gave it to the tribe of Reuben (Josh 13), and it is in ruins now and does not exist.

32.17.4.en: 2- Ataroth: it was spoken of in (v. 3), and it too has disappeared and does not exist now.

32.17.5.en: 3- Aroer: also called Ararir. After having been the portion of the tribe of Gad, it was afterward taken by the king of Aram and then the king of Moab (2 Kgs 10-32), (Jer 48:19).

32.17.6.en: 4- Atroth-shophan: it lay in the plain of Moab.

32.17.7.en: 5- Jazer: it belonged to the tribe of Gad, and Joshua afterward gave it as a portion to the sons of Merari (the Levites).

32.17.8.en: 6- Jogbehah: it is thought to be the present village of Jubeihat, which lies northwest of Amman.

32.17.9.en: 7- Beth-nimrah: it lies north of the Dead Sea.

32.17.10.en: 8- Beth-haran: it is now known as Tell er-Rameh .. and it faces Jericho, which lies west of the Jordan. These cities, after being rebuilt by the tribe of Gad, became fortified cities, and folds were also built for their cattle and sheep.

32.18.0.en: The tribe of Reuben did as their brethren of the tribe of "Gad" had done, and they rebuilt and built the cities that became their portion. They kept the names of some of them as they were, and changed others to names they gave them ... These cities were:

32.18.1.en: 1- Heshbon: the most famous of all their cities, for it was the largest of them, and it was the capital of the Amorites.

32.18.2.en: 2- Elealeh: it remained Reuben's until the Moabites afterward took it, as stated in (Isa 15:4, Jer 48:34).

32.18.3.en: 3- Kirjathaim: after Reuben rebuilt it, it afterward fell into the hands of the Moabites.

32.18.5.en: 5- Baal-meon: it was also called "Meon" and "Beth-baal-meon".

32.18.6.en: 6- Shibmah: also called "Shebam" or "Sibmah"; it is now a ruin, and in it are the remains of the stone winepresses for which it was famous.

32.19.0.en: After "Gad" and "Reuben" had each taken their portions of the land, it is mentioned here that the sons of "Machir", who was the firstborn son of Manasseh the son of Joseph, were able to cleanse some villages of the Amorites of the remnant of their inhabitants and drive them out, and for this reason Moses gave them these regions as a portion for them, that is, for the sons of Machir only.

32.20.0.en: The second portion, for the clans of the tribe of Manasseh, fell to Jair, who was originally of the tribe of Judah but joined the tribe of Manasseh by marrying a woman of the descendants of Machir the son of Manasseh. This was a strange and unusual situation in the sequence of the genealogy of the tribes, since it was usual for a woman to be reckoned to her husband's tribe, and not as happened here.

32.20.1.en: This portion that Jair had was lands famous for farms, so he took it and gave it his name, and called these farms "Havoth-jair", that is, the villages of Jair.

32.21.0.en: Nobah, also a father of clans of the tribe of Manasseh, took and seized the city of Kenath and some villages around it, and to perpetuate his name and his clans after him he gave it his name.

32.21.1.en: As the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh rebuilt cities for the dwelling of their children and wives, you should build up your life with many virtues, so that you can live with your thoughts and senses at ease, and even growing, in a pure life with God. And in proportion to how much you toil and God sees your love in your striving, He gives you many virtues.

32.21.2.en: The journeys of the children of Israel from Egypt to the east of the Jordan
